newsitem.title: USA: Families remember TWA Flight 800 one year later.
newsitem.headline: Families remember TWA Flight 800 one year later.

text.p: Hundreds of people who lost loved ones on board TWA Flight 800 gathered on Thursday for a memorial service on a beach near the site where the jumbo jet suddenly exploded a year ago.

Family and friends of victims wept and hugged as the names of the 230 dead were slowly read aloud. Haunting bagpipes played as the mourners walked to the ocean water's edge to toss rose petals into the waves.
"Time does not heal," said Richard Hammer, who lost his wife and daughter in the crash. "Time numbs."

Investigators still do not know why the Paris-bound Boeing 747 exploded over the Atlantic Ocean just 11 minutes after taking off from New York's Kennedy International Airport on July 17, 1996. They have determined that the plane's centre fuel tank exploded but do not know what triggered the blast.

This week they are flying test flights out of Kennedy, hoping to replicate conditions on board the ill-fated plane and help solve the mystery. They suspect mechanical failure but have not officially ruled out a bomb or missile as the cause of the explosion.
Key figures in the investigation, such as Robert Francis of the National Transportation Safety Board and James Kallstrom of the FBI were among those attending the beach service.
Many family members paused in front of a black marble slab in which the names of the dead have been carved. Some reached to caress an engraved name.
One man sat through the service, barely taking his eyes off a snapshot of a loved one hanging on a string around his neck. About 750 people attended the service, officials estimated.

"Everyone in the world knows of your sorrow. They know too how you have pulled together as a family," U.S. Secretary of Transportation Rodney Slater told them. "I speak for a nation when I say that in your anguish, you have lifted us."
He read a statement from President Bill Clinton, which said in part, "We met many of you last summer at this time, and each of you has remained in our thoughts throughout the past difficult year."

The consulate general of Italy, Franco Mistretta, and the consulate general of France, Patrick Gautraut, also made brief remarks to the mourners. Victims of the crash included citizens of Italy, France, Israel and other nations.
Singer Judy Collins sang "Amazing Grace," urging the mourners to sing along. "It helps to sing," she said.
After the ceremony, military jets flew in formation overhead, and U.S. Coast Guard cutters carried flowers and wreaths to drop at the site of the crash offshore.

Another memorial service was held earlier at St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York City. Another was held in Montoursville, Pennsylvania, the home town of 16 high school students and five adult chaperones who died on the plane.
Other memorials are scheduled through the weekend.
